## Why splitting is needed

For a subcritical branching process with $\lambda < \mu$, extinction is typical and
$P(\tau > T)$ becomes very small when $T$ is large. Naive direct simulation wastes
most trajectories because they hit the absorbing state $Z_t = 0$ long before $T$.

Multilevel splitting introduces times
$0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_K=T$, estimates each conditional probability
$P(\tau>t_k\mid\tau>t_{k-1})$, and multiplies them:

$$
\widehat{P}(\tau>T)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{p}_k,
\qquad
\widehat{p}_k=\frac{\#\{\text{survivors at }t_k\}}{N}.
$$

Resampling survivors at each level concentrates computation on rare surviving lineages.

## Setup

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from inf_bp_texts.simulation import (
    FlemingViotConfig,
    SplittingConfig,
    plot_conditioned_trajectories,
    plot_empirical_population_mean,
    plot_level_survival_probabilities,
    simulate_subcritical_survival_fleming_viot,
    simulate_subcritical_survival_splitting,
)
```

## Example parameters

```{python}
birth_rate = 0.9

death_rate = 1.0
terminal_time = 100.0
n_particles = 1000
n_levels = 20
random_seed = 42
```

## Run multilevel splitting

```{python}
splitting_config = SplittingConfig(
    birth_rate=birth_rate,
    death_rate=death_rate,
    terminal_time=terminal_time,
    n_particles=n_particles,
    n_levels=n_levels,
    random_seed=random_seed,
    n_conditioned_trajectories=12,
)

splitting_result = simulate_subcritical_survival_splitting(splitting_config)

print(
    f"Estimated survival probability P(tau > T): {splitting_result.survival_probability_estimate:.6e}"
)
print(f"Final survivor bank size: {splitting_result.final_survivor_count}")
print(
    "Product check: ",
    f"{np.prod(splitting_result.level_survival_probabilities):.6e}",
)
```

## Conditioned trajectories

```{python}
fig_conditioned = plot_conditioned_trajectories(
    splitting_result.conditioned_trajectories,
    max_trajectories=10,
    title="Conditioned Population Trajectories (Splitting)",
)
fig_conditioned
```

## Empirical mean population across levels

```{python}
fig_mean = plot_empirical_population_mean(
    level_times=splitting_result.level_times,
    mean_populations=splitting_result.level_mean_populations,
    title="Empirical Mean Population by Level (Splitting)",
)
fig_mean
```

## Estimated survival probabilities across levels

```{python}
fig_level_probs = plot_level_survival_probabilities(
    level_times=splitting_result.level_times,
    level_survival_probabilities=splitting_result.level_survival_probabilities,
    title="Level-wise Conditional Survival Estimates",
)
fig_level_probs
```

## Optional comparison: Fleming-Viot approximation

```{python}
fv_config = FlemingViotConfig(
    birth_rate=birth_rate,
    death_rate=death_rate,
    terminal_time=terminal_time,
    n_particles=n_particles,
    n_levels=n_levels,
    random_seed=random_seed,
    n_conditioned_trajectories=8,
)

fv_result = simulate_subcritical_survival_fleming_viot(fv_config)

comparison_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "method": ["splitting", "fleming_viot_levelwise"],
        "estimate": [
            splitting_result.survival_probability_estimate,
            fv_result.survival_proxy_estimate,
        ],
        "final_survivor_bank": [
            splitting_result.final_survivor_count,
            fv_result.final_survivor_count,
        ],
    },
)
comparison_df
```

```{python}
fig_compare_probs = plot_level_survival_probabilities(
    level_times=fv_result.level_times,
    level_survival_probabilities=fv_result.level_survival_probabilities,
    title="Level-wise Survival Proxy (Fleming-Viot)",
)
fig_compare_probs
```

## Notes on numerical stability and variance

- Too few levels can produce high variance because some $\widehat{p}_k$ are very small.
- Too many levels can increase resampling noise and computational overhead.
- A practical strategy is to choose levels so empirical survivor fractions stay away
  from both 0 and 1, then check sensitivity to level grids and random seeds.
